output.brief: The gap looks mostly like a difference in time in level, not a proximity effect. Only 32% of remote staff have the 18 months in level the policy requires, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination and approval rates are nearly the same: 20.0% remote versus 21.1% office. Applying office rates to the remote mix predicts 8.2%, against 7.6% observed. The gap also appears in every job family, so job mix isn't the cause. The remaining 1.1-point difference rests on only 110 remote staff, so a small real bias can't be ruled out. Stretch-work access is unmeasured: the staffing system can't show it. Attrition wasn't examined, so I can't say whether remote staff leave more often. I'm fairly confident about the main finding, less so about the smaller points. Don't confirm proximity bias or announce the three-day office rule. It targets the wrong cause, and about 180 remote staff on home-based contracts live too far away to comply. Instead, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Meanwhile, start tracking stretch assignments, and check why remote staff are newer. Briefings on the criteria are a reasonable low-cost addition.
